samples.summary: Comment routes bypass the per-user notification throttle that `POST /notifications/comment` deliberately enforces
samples.evidence: `notify()` calls `this.notificationService.createFromComment(actorId, plan)` in-process (comments.controller.ts:188). The only other caller of that service method, `NotificationController.createFromComment` (notification/notification.controller.ts:63-70), is guarded by `@UseGuards(UserThrottlerGuard)` + `@Throttle({ default: { ttl: 60_000, limit: 30 } })` precisely because it is "the one endpoint a client can call on its own initiative" and because IP keying "leaves an attacker with several source addresses effectively uncapped" (user-throttler.guard.ts:7-15). The new path is bounded only by the global IP-keyed bucket of 120 req/min (app.module.ts:97-104). Attack: a workspace member (or any write-scoped API key) loops `POST /api/v1/workspaces/{ws}/documents/{id}/comments` with a body containing 20 distinct `@[x](id)` mentions; each request writes up to `MAX_RECIPIENTS` (20) notification rows and pushes an SSE summary to each recipient, giving ~2400 rows/min per source IP and unbounded per user across IPs — 4x+ the rate the throttled route allows, i.e. inbox/SSE spam against every member of the workspace. `dedupeKey` is the fresh `commentId` for mention/reply events, so the unique index absorbs nothing. docs/design/notifications.md explicitly waives this ("What it is *not* subject to is `UserThrottlerGuard` ... bounded by the one-comment-per-request shape"), which is the assumption I believe is wrong.

samples.summary: Unbounded mention list from an uncapped comment body: O(n^2) dedupe and an unbounded SQL `IN (...)`, bypassing the DTO caps the HTTP path enforces
samples.evidence: `planCommentNotifications` collects every `@[..](id)` in the body with no cap (comments.controller.ts:559-566), deduping with `!mentioned.includes(id)` — a linear scan inside the match loop, so O(n^2). The resulting array is handed straight to `NotificationService.createFromComment`, which is normally reached only through `CommentNotificationDto`, whose `@ArrayMaxSize(50)` + `@IsInt({each:true})` (notification/notification.dto.ts:57-61) exist to bound exactly this; calling the service directly skips class-validator entirely. Inside the service, `memberIdsAmong(workspaceId, [actorId, ...candidates])` runs `WHERE userId IN (...)` over the whole list (notification.service.ts:126-137, 428-437) and only then applies `slice(0, MAX_RECIPIENTS)`. Attack: POST a ~25MB comment body (the configured `JSON_BODY_LIMIT`, main.ts:20) of ~1.9M distinct `@[](nnnn)` tokens; the `includes` scan alone is ~10^12 comparisons on the single-threaded event loop, blocking the whole backend process, and the Prisma query is built with far more bind parameters than Postgres accepts. The thrown error is then swallowed by `notify`'s catch (comments.controller.ts:189-195), so the abuse is invisible in responses.

samples.summary: `DELETE :threadId` / `DELETE :threadId/comments/:commentId` have no author check — any workspace member can delete another user's comments
samples.evidence: `deleteThread` (comments.controller.ts:389) and `deleteComment` (comments.controller.ts:404) only run `loadCommentableType` (workspace + type) and then `applyDeleteThread` / `applyDeleteComment`; neither compares the stored `comment.author.userId` with the caller. The product rule everywhere else is author-only: `CommentThreadCard.tsx:89-93` gates edit/delete on `c.author.userId === currentUserId`, and `packages/frontend/src/app/shared/shared-document.tsx:902` refers to that gate as the rule. So any workspace member — including a write-scoped API key minted by any member — can silently destroy an entire review thread authored by someone else, and deleting the opening comment cascades to the whole thread (`applyDeleteComment` -> `thread_deleted`). Confidence is low because comments live only in the CRDT: a malicious editor client can already write the same deletion directly, so the UI check was never server-enforced and this route may be considered to match the real capability rather than widen it. Note the manager tier (`document-access.ts:16`) is not the right analogue either — it gates document delete/move, not content edits.

samples.summary: No maximum length on a comment body written through the API
samples.evidence: `normalizeBody` (yorkie/comment-ops.ts, used at comments.controller.ts:251 and :336) only rejects non-strings and whitespace-only values; there is no length ceiling, so a single authenticated write can push up to the 25MB `JSON_BODY_LIMIT` (main.ts:20) of text into a shared Yorkie document, which is then replicated to every connected editor client and re-scanned in full by `sanitizePreview`'s three regex passes (notification.service.ts:67-82) on every notification. Compare the notification DTO, which caps `preview` at 2000 chars. This is a storage/bandwidth amplification available to any workspace member with a write-scoped credential, and it compounds the mention-parsing cost above.

samples.summary: Raw mention tokens are sent as the notification preview, leaking the encoded userId the frontend deliberately strips
samples.evidence: `planCommentNotifications` sets `preview: comment.body` (comments.controller.ts:572 and :588) — the raw body including `@[username](userId)` tokens. The frontend equivalent this claims to mirror flattens first: `preview()` uses `mentionBodyToPlainText(body)` (frontend/src/components/comments/notify.ts:35-37), and `mentionBodyToPlainText`'s docblock states the reason outright — "the raw token must not leak" (frontend/src/components/comments/mentions.ts:119-123). `sanitizePreview` only strips control characters and truncates, so every recipient of an API-authored mention/reply sees internal numeric `User.id`s of the other mentioned users in their notification dropdown. Low impact (recipients are workspace members who can already enumerate members) but it is an information-disclosure regression against an explicitly documented rule.

samples.summary: `parseImages` accepts any non-empty string as an image `src` — no scheme or origin restriction
samples.evidence: `src: requireString(i.src, 'src')` (worksheet-images.ts:55) is the only check; `anchor` is validated against `parseRef` and the sizes are range-checked, but the URL is not. A write-scoped API key can therefore place `src: "https://attacker.example/px.gif"` (or a `data:`/`blob:` value) on any sheet tab, and every later viewer's browser — including anonymous share-link viewers — fetches it, disclosing viewer IP/User-Agent/timing to a host of the attacker's choosing. Two mitigations keep this minor rather than major: the frontend refuses to append a share token to a non-backend origin (`isTrustedWorkspaceImageUrl`, frontend/src/api/share-image-url.ts:27-42, which documents this exact threat), and nothing server-side fetches `src` (the copy path matches it against an anchored workspace-image path regex and only rehosts same-workspace refs, document/document-image-refs.ts:33-34,113), so there is no SSRF. The editor CRDT path has the same hole, so this is hardening on a newly remote-reachable write.

samples.summary: New `unwrapJson` fallback routes malformed CRDT values into `detachYorkieValue`, which recurses with no depth bound
samples.evidence: The change makes `unwrapJson` fall back to `detachYorkieValue(value)` when the repaired parse still fails (yorkie-json.ts:21-24). `detachYorkieValue` (yorkie-json.ts:149-182) recurses over arrays and objects with no depth ceiling, unlike the sibling walker in document/document-image-refs.ts:12-16, whose `MAX_DEPTH = 64` exists explicitly to bound "the one thing a hostile or corrupt document could otherwise do here, which is blow the stack". A sufficiently deeply nested value in a worksheet's `images` map or a board root (reachable by a malicious collaborator writing the CRDT directly; the API path is capped at `MAX_ELEMENT_DEPTH = 32`) turns a read into a `RangeError` 500 rather than a clean error. Impact is limited to a per-request failure, and the recursive walker predates this change — the diff only widens where it is reached from.

verdict.reason: All cited code is present as described. comments.controller.ts:188 calls NotificationService.createFromComment in-process from createThread (:290,:320), reply (:351) and setResolved (:383); the controller carries only CombinedAuthGuard/WorkspaceScopeGuard/ApiKeyWriteScopeGuard (:95) and no @Throttle or UserThrottlerGuard (grep shows the guard is used only at notification.controller.ts:64 and template.controller.ts:178/218). The sibling client-initiated path notification.controller.ts:63-71 is throttled per user at 30/min precisely because IP keying is bypassable (user-throttler.guard.ts:7-15), while the new path is bounded only by the global IP-keyed 120/min bucket (app.module.ts:97-104,128-129). Fan-out is real and undeduped: up to MAX_RECIPIENTS=20 rows per plan and two plans per request (notification.service.ts:12,136-152; planCommentNotifications), each triggering an SSE summary push (notification.service.ts:389-425), and dedupeKeyFor (:90-98) uses the fresh commentId so the unique index absorbs nothing. Authorization itself is still enforced (membership checks at notification.service.ts:126-138), so this is not an authz bypass — but a deliberately-introduced per-user rate-limit control on the same operation is absent on a second, equally attacker-controlled entry point, which falls under access-control (missing/ineffective rate limiting) rather than general correctness. No guard, interceptor, or module-level throttle makes the path unreachable, so I have no named ground to refute.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding is present as described. `normalizeBody` (comment-ops.ts:277-280) imposes no length cap, so a comment body limited only by the 25MB `JSON_BODY_LIMIT` (main.ts:20) flows into `notify` (comments.controller.ts:290-293, 320-323, 351-354). `planCommentNotifications` (comments.controller.ts:558-564) collects mention ids with an uncapped loop that dedupes via `!mentioned.includes(id)` — a linear scan per match, i.e. O(n^2) on the single-threaded event loop — and pushes the whole array as `recipientUserIds` (:566-573). The `@ArrayNotEmpty/@ArrayMaxSize(50)/@IsInt({each:true})` bound on that field (notification/notification.dto.ts:57-61) is enforced only by the global ValidationPipe on HTTP bodies (main.ts:65-72); the controller builds the DTO in-process and calls `notificationService.createFromComment` directly (comments.controller.ts:188), so class-validator never runs — a real bypass of an existing validation gate at a non-HTTP call site. Inside the service the unbounded list is sent to Postgres as `userId: { in: unique(userIds) }` (notification.service.ts:126-129, 428-437) and `MAX_RECIPIENTS = 20` (:12) is applied only afterwards (:136-138). The resulting throw is swallowed by the warn-only catch (comments.controller.ts:189-195), so abuse is invisible to the caller. Reachable by any authenticated workspace member / write-scoped API key (comments.controller.ts:94-95). No upstream cap or guard makes it unreachable, and untrusted-input-driven resource exhaustion plus a bypassed input-validation gate is within the security lane (not in the excluded list).

verdict.reason: The factual absence is real - I confirmed no author check in deleteThread/deleteComment (comments.controller.ts:388-431), none in applyDeleteThread/applyDeleteComment (comment-ops.ts:238-263), and the only global guard is the throttler (app.module.ts:128) - so I found no counterexample. But it is not a blocking security defect under this lens, because it crosses no trust boundary. The route is reachable only by workspace members: WorkspaceScopeGuard requires live membership for JWT callers and for the user who minted an API key (workspace-scope.guard.ts:40-45), and anonymous share-token traffic is explicitly excluded (workspace-scope.guard.ts:24-26). Every such member already holds unrestricted read-write on the document CRDT with no field-level authorization ("Membership grants read+write; the model has no per-member viewer role today", yorkie-auth.controller.ts:193-206), and comment deletion over that path is likewise unguarded: the editor's own store deletes any thread/comment as a plain map mutation with the same index-0 thread cascade (yorkie-comment-store.ts:246-257). The CommentThreadCard.tsx:89-92 author test is a UI affordance inside that same client, bypassable by the member's own session. An API key is a strict subset of its minter's authority. So the route grants no capability the caller lacks - the same actor can already delete the thread, and indeed all document content, through the enforced path. Author-only comment deletion is not server-enforced anywhere in the product, so no gate is weakened, bypassed, or moved out of the enforced path; adding enforcement would be a new restriction rather than restoration of one. That makes it a consistency/hardening item (minor at most); whether the product rule ought to be enforced server-side is a correctness/product-fit call outside the security lane.
